title: Staying off methamphetamine: recovery over a year
description: Heavy methamphetamine use reduces the dopamine transporters in the striatum, a marker of the dopamine nerve endings that carry reward signals. One study scanned people early in recovery and again after more than a year without the drug. The transporters had partly come back. In this episode brightness stands for the amount of dopamine transporter, not activity. In the first part it shows the loss compared with people who do not use drugs; in "What changed" it shows the change since early recovery.
caveat: This is one small study: five people, all in a court-supervised rehabilitation programme, who stayed off the drug for over a year, scanned twice with PET. The loss shown in the first part is the 24-30% loss the same group reported earlier. Recovery of the transporters did not bring equal recovery in memory and movement tests. It is about methamphetamine only, and about staying off it, not a specific treatment. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: In early recovery, the dopamine transporters in the striatum are about a quarter lower than in people who do not use drugs.

phases.name: More than a year drug-free
phases.caption: Staying off the drug, with regular drug testing. The brain is drawn at rest here.

citations.authors: Volkow ND, Chang L, Wang GJ, Fowler JS, Franceschi D, Sedler M, Gatley SJ, et al.
citations.title: Loss of dopamine transporters in methamphetamine abusers recovers with protracted abstinence.
citations.quote: Five METH abusers (three females, two males; 29 ± 3 years of age) were evaluated twice: during early (mean ± SD, 3 ± 1.6 months of abstinence) and then at least 9 months later during protracted abstinence (mean ± SD, 14 ± 2 months).

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: After more than a year without the drug, the transporters have increased: by about 19% in the caudate and 16% in the putamen.

citations.authors: Volkow ND, Chang L, Wang GJ, Fowler JS, Franceschi D, Sedler M, Gatley SJ, et al.
citations.title: Loss of dopamine transporters in methamphetamine abusers recovers with protracted abstinence.
citations.quote: Five METH abusers (three females, two males; 29 ± 3 years of age) were evaluated twice: during early (mean ± SD, 3 ± 1.6 months of abstinence) and then at least 9 months later during protracted abstinence (mean ± SD, 14 ± 2 months).

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: Memory and movement tests did not improve to the same extent, so the recovery was not complete. The authors conclude that staying off the drug may reverse some of the changes, not all of them.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: Dopamine transporters were about a quarter lower than in people who do not use drugs early in recovery, and rose by 19% after more than a year without the drug, in one study of five people. Brightness stands for the amount of transporter, not activity.

citations.title: Loss of dopamine transporters in methamphetamine abusers recovers with protracted abstinence.
citations.quote: Although the DAT loss reported in METH abusers (24–30%) is smaller than that reported in Parkinson's disease (36 and 71%) (Frost et al., 1993; Innis et al., 1993), it is nonetheless associated with reduced motor speed and impaired verbal learning (Volkow et al., 2001).

citations.authors: Volkow ND, Chang L, Wang GJ, Fowler JS, Franceschi D, Sedler M, Gatley SJ, et al.
citations.title: Loss of dopamine transporters in methamphetamine abusers recovers with protracted abstinence.
citations.quote: Brain DA transporters in five methamphetamine abusers evaluated during short abstinence (<6 months) and then retested during protracted abstinence (12–17 months) showed significant increases with protracted abstinence (caudate, +19%; putamen, +16%).
